decks.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants — Part 1: The flower and its gametophytes
goals: Describe the structure of the stamen, anther and microsporangium
Explain microsporogenesis and the structure of a pollen grain
Describe the pistil and the parts of an ovule
Explain megasporogenesis and the development of the embryo sac

slides.heading: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
slides.body_md: Part 1 — inside the stamen and the pistil: how a flower makes its male and female gametophytes before pollination.

nodes.label: Pistil: ovule with embryo sac (female gametophyte)

visual.alt: Flow from the flower to stamen and pistil, then pollination, double fertilisation, and seed and fruit

slides.narration: Every mango you eat and every grain of rice began inside a flower. A flower is not just decoration. It is the reproductive organ of flowering plants. In this part we open up the stamen and the pistil, and follow how tiny male and female structures form long before any pollen reaches a stigma.

slides.heading: The flower: events before fertilisation
slides.body_md: Long before a flower opens, its fate is decided by **hormonal and structural changes** that turn a shoot apex into a floral bud. Inside the bud, the **androecium** (whorl of stamens) and the **gynoecium** (pistils) develop.

visual.alt: Table comparing the male and female sides of a flower: whorl, spore-forming organ, mother cell, gametophyte and gametes

slides.narration: Think of the flower as having two production lines. The male line runs through the stamens and ends with pollen grains. The female line runs through the pistil and ends with the embryo sac inside each ovule. Keep this two-column picture in mind; almost every term in this part fits into one of the two columns.

slides.heading: Stamen and anther
slides.body_md: A **stamen** has a long **filament** and a terminal, usually **bilobed** anther. Each lobe has **two thecae**, so a typical anther is **dithecous** and holds **four microsporangia** at its corners. The microsporangia later become **pollen sacs**.

slides.narration: Look at the left drawing. A young anther cut across looks like four rounded chambers, two in each lobe, held together by a central connective that carries a vascular bundle. Each chamber is a microsporangium. When the anther matures, these chambers fill with pollen, and that is why we also call them pollen sacs.

slides.heading: Wall layers of a microsporangium
slides.body_md: In section, a microsporangium looks almost circular. Its wall has **four layers**; the outer three protect the sac and help it split open (**dehiscence**); the innermost, the **tapetum**, feeds the developing pollen.

rows: Protection; helps the anther split to release pollen
Nourishes developing pollen; cells have dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus

visual.alt: Table of the four wall layers of a microsporangium from outside to inside with their roles

slides.narration: Remember the order from outside in: epidermis, endothecium, middle layers, tapetum. The first three are like the walls of a storeroom: they protect the contents and later crack open to release pollen. The tapetum is the kitchen. Its cells are packed with cytoplasm and often have more than one nucleus, because they work hard to feed the growing pollen.

slides.heading: Microsporogenesis
slides.body_md: While the anther is young, the centre of each microsporangium is filled with compactly arranged **sporogenous tissue**. Each of these cells can act as a **microspore mother cell** (pollen mother cell). It undergoes **meiosis** to form a cluster of four haploid cells, the **microspore tetrad**.

visual.alt: Flow of microsporogenesis from sporogenous cell to microspore mother cell, meiosis to a tetrad, and separation into pollen grains

slides.narration: Microsporogenesis simply means the making of microspores. One diploid mother cell divides by meiosis and gives four haploid microspores, still stuck together as a tetrad. As the anther matures and loses water, the four separate and each develops into a pollen grain. So every single meiosis gives exactly four pollen grains, a fact you will use in calculations.

slides.heading: The pollen grain
slides.body_md: Pollen grains are usually spherical, about **25–50 micrometres** across. The hard outer **exine** is made of **sporopollenin**, one of the most resistant organic materials known: it survives high temperature and strong acids and alkalis, and no known enzyme breaks it down. Where sporopollenin is absent, the exine has **germ pores**. The thin inner **intine** is of cellulose and pectin.

slides.narration: A pollen grain is a tiny survival capsule. Its outer wall, the exine, is made of sporopollenin, which is so tough that pollen is preserved as fossils for millions of years. The wall has gaps called germ pores, and that is where the pollen tube will later grow out. Inside the exine sits a thin, soft layer called the intine.

slides.heading: Inside a mature pollen grain
slides.body_md: A mature pollen grain holds **two cells**: a large **vegetative cell** with abundant food reserve and an irregular nucleus, and a small, spindle-shaped **generative cell** floating in its cytoplasm. The generative cell divides by **mitosis** to form the **two male gametes**.

rows: Vegetative cell + generative cell; the generative cell divides later, in the pollen tube

visual.alt: Table comparing two-celled and three-celled pollen grains at shedding and how common each is

slides.narration: Here is the key point. The vegetative cell is the big one; it stores food and will grow the pollen tube. The generative cell is small. In most flowering plants, more than sixty percent, pollen is shed at the two-celled stage and the generative cell divides inside the pollen tube. In the rest, it divides before shedding, so the pollen is three-celled.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting pollen grains
slides.body_md: An anther has 4 microsporangia, and each contains 45 microspore mother cells. How many pollen grains can the anther produce, and how many meiotic divisions does this need?
bullets: Step 1 — Mother cells in the anther $= 4 \times 45 = 180$.
Step 2 — Each mother cell undergoes **one meiosis** and gives **4** microspores.
Step 3 — Pollen grains $= 180 \times 4 = 720$; meiotic divisions $= 180$.
Check — working backwards, $720 \div 4 = 180$ meioses.

visual.alt: Worked table: 4 microsporangia with 45 mother cells each give 180 meioses and 720 pollen grains

slides.narration: Count the mother cells first: four chambers times forty-five cells gives one hundred and eighty. Each mother cell undergoes one meiosis and gives four pollen grains, so the anther can make seven hundred and twenty pollen grains from one hundred and eighty meiotic divisions. Always remember: one meiosis, four pollen grains.

slides.heading: Pollen and people
slides.body_md: Pollen matters beyond the flower: it can trigger **allergies**, it is a **food supplement**, and it can be **stored** for plant breeding.

rows: Pollen of many plants, for example carrot grass (Parthenium), can cause asthma and bronchitis
Pollen is rich in nutrients and is sold as tablets and syrups
Rice and wheat pollen lose viability within about 30 minutes; pollen of some rose, pea and potato family members stays viable for months
Pollen can be kept for years in liquid nitrogen at about −196 °C, in pollen banks for crop breeding

visual.alt: Table of pollen facts on allergy, nutrition, viability and storage

slides.narration: Carrot grass, called Parthenium, arrived in India with imported wheat and spread everywhere; its pollen causes allergies in many people. Pollen is also eaten as a health supplement. How long pollen stays alive varies hugely: in rice and wheat only about half an hour, but in some plants for months. Breeders store pollen in liquid nitrogen for years.

slides.heading: The pistil and the ovule
slides.body_md: A **pistil** has a **stigma** (landing platform for pollen), a **style** and a swollen **ovary**. A gynoecium may have one pistil (**monocarpellary**) or many (**multicarpellary**); several pistils may be fused (**syncarpous**, as in poppy) or free (**apocarpous**, as in Michelia). Inside the ovary, **ovules** (megasporangia) arise from the **placenta**.

visual.caption: Schematic, not to scale.

slides.narration: An ovule is attached to the placenta by a stalk, the funicle. The point where the ovule body joins the funicle is the hilum. One or two protective integuments wrap around the ovule but leave a small opening, the micropyle. Opposite it lies the chalaza, the base of the ovule. Inside the integuments is the nucellus, and inside the nucellus sits the embryo sac.

slides.heading: Megasporogenesis
slides.body_md: A single **megaspore mother cell**, large and with dense cytoplasm, differentiates in the **micropylar region of the nucellus**. It undergoes **meiosis** to form **four megaspores**. In most flowering plants **one megaspore is functional** and the other three degenerate. An embryo sac formed from a single megaspore is called **monosporic**.

visual.alt: Flow of megasporogenesis: megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to form four megaspores, three degenerate and one is functional

slides.narration: Compare this with the anther. There, every meiosis gives four useful pollen grains. Here, one mother cell gives four megaspores, but in most plants only one survives and the other three degenerate. So each ovule usually contains just one functional megaspore, and that single cell will build the entire female gametophyte.

slides.heading: Building the embryo sac
slides.body_md: The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides by **mitosis** three times, without cell walls at first (**free nuclear** divisions): 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 nuclei. Then walls form. Six nuclei are enclosed in cells; the remaining **two polar nuclei** sit in the large **central cell**.

rows: One nucleus from each pole moves to the centre as a polar nucleus

visual.alt: Table of the three free nuclear mitoses giving two, four and eight nuclei, then wall formation giving seven cells

slides.narration: Three rounds of mitosis turn one nucleus into eight. Four nuclei end up at each end. Then one nucleus from each end travels to the middle; these two are the polar nuclei. Walls now form around the six nuclei at the ends. The result is a sac with seven cells but eight nuclei, because the central cell holds two.

slides.heading: The mature embryo sac
slides.body_md: At the **micropylar end**, three cells form the **egg apparatus**: two **synergids** and one **egg cell**. Synergids carry special thickenings at their micropylar tip, the **filiform apparatus**, which guides the pollen tube. At the **chalazal end** are three **antipodal** cells. The large **central cell** holds the two polar nuclei.

visual.caption: Seven cells, eight nuclei.

slides.narration: Learn this picture well; examiners love it. At the micropyle end sits the egg apparatus: the egg cell with two synergids beside it. The synergids have a brush-like filiform apparatus that guides the pollen tube in. Three antipodal cells sit at the far, chalazal end. The central cell, with its two polar nuclei, fills the middle.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: who carries how many chromosomes?
slides.body_md: A plant has 18 chromosomes in each leaf cell. Find the chromosome number in its megaspore mother cell, functional megaspore, egg, synergid, antipodal cell, each polar nucleus, nucellus cell and integument cell.
bullets: Step 1 — Leaf cells are diploid, so $2n = 18$ and $n = 9$.
Step 2 — The megaspore mother cell, nucellus and integuments are **sporophyte** tissue: 18 each.
Step 3 — The megaspore is made by **meiosis**, and every cell of the embryo sac comes from it by **mitosis**, so each has 9.
Conclusion — everything inside the embryo sac is haploid; everything around it is diploid.

rows: Egg, synergid, antipodal, each polar nucleus

visual.alt: Worked table: sporophyte cells have 18 chromosomes; the megaspore and every embryo sac nucleus have 9

slides.narration: Sort every cell into one of two groups. Cells of the parent plant, like the nucellus and integuments, are diploid, eighteen here. The megaspore comes from meiosis, so it has nine, and all the embryo sac nuclei come from it by mitosis, so they also have nine. Each polar nucleus is haploid; they only become part of a triploid nucleus after fertilisation.

slides.heading: Quick check: count the embryo sac
slides.body_md: How many cells and nuclei does a typical mature embryo sac have?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the cells at each end, then the central cell, and remember that one cell holds two nuclei.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Anther: usually bilobed and dithecous, with **four microsporangia**; wall of epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and **tapetum** (nourishes pollen).
**Microsporogenesis:** microspore mother cell → meiosis → tetrad → four pollen grains.
Pollen: **exine** of sporopollenin with germ pores, **intine** of cellulose and pectin; vegetative cell + generative cell (two male gametes by mitosis).
Ovule: funicle, hilum, integuments, micropyle, chalaza, nucellus, embryo sac.
**Megasporogenesis:** one mother cell → meiosis → four megaspores → one functional (monosporic).
Three free nuclear mitoses → **8 nuclei, 7 cells**: egg apparatus (egg + 2 synergids), 3 antipodals, central cell with 2 polar nuclei.

visual.alt: Summary table comparing the male and female gametophytes

slides.narration: Let us recap. The anther makes pollen through microsporogenesis, and the tapetum feeds it. The pollen wall has a tough exine and a soft intine. In the ovule, one megaspore survives and three rounds of mitosis build a seven-celled, eight-nucleate embryo sac. Now the stage is set for pollination, the subject of Part 2.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Draw and label the **embryo sac** with the micropylar end at the bottom; label both ends and the filiform apparatus.
Write "**seven-celled, eight-nucleate**" for the embryo sac; examiners look for both numbers.
Pollen counts: **one meiosis gives four pollen grains**; one ovule usually needs **one meiosis** for its megaspore.
Ploidy: cells inside the embryo sac and the pollen are **haploid**; nucellus, integuments and mother cells are **diploid**.
Do not confuse **monosporic** (one megaspore forms the sac) with monoecious (both sexes on one plant).
slides.narration: Three quick tips. First, label the embryo sac with both ends named. Second, in counting questions, one meiosis gives four pollen grains but only one functional megaspore. Third, for ploidy questions, ask whether a cell belongs to the parent plant or to the gametophyte. That one question sorts out almost every case.

slides.heading: Pollination
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how pollen, which cannot move by itself, reaches a stigma, and how plants encourage cross-pollination.

visual.alt: Flow from anther dehiscence to pollen transfer, landing on the stigma and acceptance or rejection

slides.narration: Male and female gametes in plants cannot walk or swim to each other. Pollen must be carried to a stigma, and that transfer is called pollination. Plants have evolved remarkable ways to get it done, using wind, water and animals, and clever tricks to avoid pollinating themselves. Let us see how.

slides.heading: Three kinds of pollination
slides.body_md: **Autogamy:** pollen reaches the stigma of the **same flower**. **Geitonogamy:** pollen reaches **another flower of the same plant**. **Xenogamy:** pollen reaches a flower of a **different plant**.

slides.narration: Geitonogamy is a tricky case. It looks like cross-pollination because an agent carries pollen from one flower to another. But both flowers belong to the same plant, so genetically it is just like self-pollination. Only xenogamy brings in genetically different pollen, and that is what creates new combinations of characters.

slides.heading: Open and closed flowers
slides.body_md: For **autogamy**, anther dehiscence and stigma receptivity must coincide, and anther and stigma must be close. Some plants, such as Viola (common pansy), Oxalis and Commelina, make **two kinds of flowers**.

visual.alt: Table comparing chasmogamous and cleistogamous flowers

slides.narration: Cleistogamous flowers never open, so pollen from their own anthers falls onto their own stigma inside the closed bud. This guarantees seeds even when no pollinator visits. The price is variation: offspring of such seeds are almost copies of the parent. That is why these plants keep both kinds of flowers.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the pollination
slides.body_md: Classify each event as autogamy, geitonogamy or xenogamy.
bullets: P — Pollen from the tassel of a maize plant lands on the silks of a cob on the **same plant**: two flowers, one plant → **geitonogamy**.
Q — A closed flower of Commelina sets seed: pollen and stigma of the **same flower** → **autogamy**.
R — A bee carries pollen from a male papaya tree to a female papaya tree: **two plants** → **xenogamy**.
S — A bisexual pea flower is pollinated by its own anthers before opening → **autogamy**.

visual.alt: Worked table classifying four pollination events by the number of flowers and plants involved

slides.narration: Use two counts. How many flowers? How many plants? One flower is autogamy. Two flowers on one plant is geitonogamy. Two plants is xenogamy. Notice that papaya must be xenogamous, because male and female flowers grow on separate trees.

slides.heading: Quick check: is geitonogamy really cross-pollination?
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about geitonogamy.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about where the pollen comes from genetically, not just which flower it comes from.

slides.heading: Agents of pollination
slides.body_md: Plants use **abiotic** agents (wind, water) and **biotic** agents (animals). Most plants use animals; only a small number use abiotic agents.

rows: Bees, butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, moths
Bees are the dominant biotic agents
Sunbirds, hummingbirds, bats; some primates, lizards and rodents

visual.alt: Table of pollination agents: wind, water, insects and other animals, with examples

slides.narration: Abiotic pollination is a matter of chance, so wind and water pollinated plants produce enormous numbers of pollen grains. Animals are far more targeted. Bees are the champion pollinators, but sunbirds, bats and even some lizards, rodents and primates carry pollen too.

slides.heading: Wind pollination
slides.body_md: Wind-pollinated flowers are built to release pollen into the air and to catch it.

rows: Pollen is shed into the wind
A single ovule in each ovary
Many flowers packed in an inflorescence

visual.alt: Table of features of wind-pollinated flowers and why each helps

slides.narration: Picture a maize field. The tassel at the top sheds clouds of light, dry pollen. The cob below has long silky threads hanging out; each thread is a stigma and style, waving in the wind to catch pollen. The flowers are dull and have no scent or nectar, because there is no animal to attract.

slides.heading: Water pollination
slides.body_md: Water pollination is rare: about **30 genera**, mostly monocots. Many aquatic plants, such as **water hyacinth** and **water lily**, still use insects or wind.

rows: Female flowers reach the surface on long stalks; male flowers or pollen float on the surface and drift to them
Female flowers stay submerged; long, ribbon-like pollen is carried inside the water
Pollen is protected from wetting by a mucilaginous covering

visual.alt: Table of water pollination in Vallisneria and seagrasses, and the mucilage covering on pollen

slides.narration: Vallisneria shows the clever version. Its female flower rises to the water surface on a long, coiled stalk. Male flowers break free and float on the surface; if one drifts against a female flower, pollen reaches the stigma. Seagrasses do it under water with long ribbon-shaped pollen. In every case, a slimy coating keeps the pollen from getting soaked.

slides.heading: Insect and animal pollination
slides.body_md: Animal-pollinated flowers **advertise** and **reward**. The pollinator gets food or shelter; the plant gets its pollen carried.

rows: Large, colourful, fragrant flowers rich in nectar
Small flowers clustered into a showy head
Flowers visited by flies and beetles
A safe place to lay eggs
Amorphophallus, one of the tallest flowers
Yucca and its moth: the moth lays eggs in the ovary; the larvae eat some seeds

visual.alt: Table of features and rewards of animal-pollinated flowers with examples

slides.narration: Yucca and its moth cannot live without each other. The moth pollinates the flower and lays its eggs in the ovary. The larvae hatch and eat some of the developing seeds, but plenty are left for the plant. Not every visitor is honest, though. Some insects take nectar or pollen without pollinating; they are called pollen or nectar robbers.

slides.heading: Quick check: spot the wind flower
slides.body_md: Which set of features best fits a wind-pollinated flower?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what a flower needs if nobody is coming to visit it.

slides.heading: Outbreeding devices
slides.body_md: Continued self-pollination causes **inbreeding depression**. Plants have evolved **outbreeding devices** that discourage self-pollination and encourage cross-pollination.

rows: Pollen is released before the stigma is receptive, or after it stops being receptive
Anther and stigma placed apart, so pollen cannot reach the stigma of the same flower
A genetic mechanism stops pollen from germinating or growing on the pistil of the same flower or plant
Male and female flowers separate: on one plant (monoecious) or on different plants (dioecious)

visual.alt: Table of four outbreeding devices and how each works

slides.narration: Why would a plant avoid its own pollen? Because repeated self-pollination makes harmful recessive traits show up, and the plants become weaker; this is inbreeding depression. So flowers mistime pollen release, keep anther and stigma apart, chemically reject their own pollen, or separate male and female flowers altogether.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which device stops which pollination?
slides.body_md: Castor and maize are **monoecious**; papaya is **dioecious**. Which kinds of self-pollination does each prevent?
bullets: Step 1 — In both, a flower is either male or female, so pollen can never land on the stigma of the **same flower**: **autogamy is prevented** in all three.
Step 2 — In castor and maize, male and female flowers are on the **same plant**, so pollen can still move between them: **geitonogamy is possible**.
Step 3 — In papaya, male and female flowers are on **different plants**: both autogamy and geitonogamy are prevented, so only **xenogamy** can happen.

visual.alt: Worked table: monoecious castor and maize prevent autogamy but not geitonogamy; dioecious papaya prevents both

slides.narration: This comparison is a favourite exam question. Unisexual flowers always rule out autogamy, because no single flower has both anthers and a stigma. But only when the sexes are on different plants is geitonogamy ruled out too. So dioecy is the strongest guarantee of cross-pollination.

slides.heading: Pollen–pistil interaction
slides.body_md: Not every pollen grain that lands on a stigma can fertilise. The pistil **recognises** compatible pollen of the right species, through chemical signals between pollen and pistil, and **promotes** it; it **inhibits** incompatible pollen.

nodes.label: Compatible: pollen germinates through a germ pore
Pollen tube grows through stigma and style to the ovary
Tube enters the ovule through the micropyle
Filiform apparatus guides it into a synergid
Incompatible: germination or tube growth is stopped

visual.alt: Flow of pollen–pistil interaction: recognition, then germination and tube growth to the synergid for compatible pollen, or rejection for incompatible pollen

slides.narration: Think of the stigma as a security desk. Every pollen grain must pass a chemical check. Compatible pollen is allowed in: it germinates, and its tube grows down the style, into the ovary, through the micropyle, and is steered by the filiform apparatus into a synergid. Incompatible pollen is stopped. In some plants you can watch pollen germinate on a glass slide in sugar and boric acid solution.

slides.heading: Quick check: the pollen tube’s route
slides.body_md: Through which opening does the pollen tube usually enter the ovule?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the small opening left by the integuments, near the egg apparatus.

slides.heading: Artificial hybridisation
slides.body_md: Breeders cross chosen parents so that only the **desired pollen** reaches the stigma. Two steps protect the stigma: **emasculation** and **bagging**.

nodes.label: Emasculation: remove anthers from the bud before they dehisce
Bagging: cover with a butter-paper bag
Stigma becomes receptive: dust it with chosen pollen
Rebag and let the fruit develop

visual.alt: Flow of artificial hybridisation: emasculation, bagging, dusting with chosen pollen, and rebagging

slides.narration: If the flower is bisexual, its own anthers must be removed with forceps while it is still a bud, before they release pollen; this is emasculation. Then the flower is covered with a butter-paper bag so stray pollen cannot reach it. When the stigma is ready, the breeder dusts it with pollen from the chosen father plant and bags it again. Female flowers of unisexual plants need no emasculation, only bagging.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Autogamy (same flower), geitonogamy (another flower, same plant: genetically like autogamy), xenogamy (different plant).
Cleistogamous flowers never open: assured seed set, little variation.
Wind: light pollen, exposed stamens, feathery stigma, one ovule per ovary. Water: Vallisneria, Zostera; mucilage-covered pollen.
Animal pollination: colour, scent, nectar, pollen, shelter; Yucca–moth partnership.
Outbreeding devices: timing, position, self-incompatibility, unisexual flowers (dioecy prevents both autogamy and geitonogamy).
Pollen–pistil interaction: recognition, then promotion or inhibition. Hybridisation: emasculation, bagging, rebagging.

visual.alt: Summary table: only xenogamy brings genetically different pollen; geitonogamy and xenogamy need an agent

slides.narration: To recap: three kinds of pollination, only xenogamy brings in new genes. Wind, water and animals each shape flowers in their own way. Outbreeding devices protect against inbreeding depression, the pistil screens every pollen grain, and breeders use emasculation and bagging to control crosses. Next, in Part 3, we follow the pollen tube into the embryo sac.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always say **why** geitonogamy is "functionally cross but genetically self".
For "monoecious versus dioecious", state which of autogamy and geitonogamy each prevents.
Water pollination: name **Vallisneria** and **Zostera**, and mention that water hyacinth and water lily are **not** water pollinated.
Hybridisation answers need both steps: **emasculation** (only for bisexual flowers) and **bagging**, with the reason for each.
slides.narration: Exam tips. When you mention geitonogamy, add the reason it is genetically like self-pollination. For unisexual flowers, separate the two kinds of self-pollination clearly. And in hybridisation questions, give both steps with their purpose: emasculation removes the flower’s own pollen, bagging keeps out unwanted pollen.

goals: Explain double fertilisation and the products of syngamy and triple fusion
Describe the development of endosperm and embryo, and compare dicot and monocot embryos
Describe how the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary a fruit
Explain apomixis, polyembryony and parthenocarpy and their uses

slides.heading: Double fertilisation and after
slides.body_md: Part 3 — what happens when the pollen tube reaches the embryo sac, and how an ovule becomes a seed and an ovary becomes a fruit.

visual.alt: Flow from pollen tube entry to double fertilisation, endosperm and embryo, seed and fruit

slides.narration: The pollen tube has found its way to the embryo sac. What happens next is unique to flowering plants: not one fertilisation but two, at the same time. After that, the ovule becomes a seed, the ovary becomes a fruit, and a new plant waits inside, ready to grow.

slides.heading: Into the embryo sac
slides.body_md: The pollen tube enters one of the **synergids** and releases **two male gametes** into its cytoplasm. Each gamete has a different partner.

visual.alt: Flow: the pollen tube releases two male gametes; one fuses with the egg, the other with the polar nuclei

slides.narration: Once inside the synergid, the tube bursts and releases its two male gametes. They do not compete; they share the work. One heads for the egg cell. The other moves into the central cell to meet the two polar nuclei. Both fusions happen in the same embryo sac.

slides.heading: Syngamy and triple fusion
slides.body_md: **Syngamy:** one male gamete fuses with the egg nucleus → diploid **zygote**. **Triple fusion:** the other male gamete fuses with the **two polar nuclei** → triploid **primary endosperm nucleus**; the central cell becomes the **primary endosperm cell**. Two fusions in one embryo sac = **double fertilisation**.

slides.narration: Syngamy is the true fertilisation: male gamete plus egg gives a diploid zygote, which will become the embryo. Triple fusion involves three haploid nuclei, one male gamete and two polar nuclei, so the product is triploid. This primary endosperm nucleus will build the endosperm, a food store for the embryo.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ploidy after double fertilisation
slides.body_md: In a plant, the root tip cells have 24 chromosomes. Find the chromosome number in the male gamete, zygote, primary endosperm nucleus, endosperm cell, embryo cell and seed coat cell.
bullets: Step 1 — Root cells are diploid: $2n = 24$, so $n = 12$; a male gamete has 12.
Step 2 — Zygote $= n + n = 12 + 12 = 24$; embryo cells come from it by mitosis: 24.
Step 3 — Primary endosperm nucleus $= n + n + n = 36$; endosperm cells: 36.
Step 4 — The seed coat comes from the integuments of the **mother plant**: 24.

visual.alt: Worked table of chromosome numbers: male gamete 12, zygote and embryo 24, endosperm 36, seed coat 24

slides.narration: Add up the nuclei that fused. The zygote has two haploid sets, so twenty-four. The primary endosperm nucleus has three, so thirty-six, and the endosperm keeps that number. The seed coat is a trap: it is not a product of fertilisation at all. It comes from the integuments of the mother plant, so it is diploid.

slides.heading: Quick check: product of triple fusion
slides.body_md: What does triple fusion produce?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count the nuclei that fuse in the central cell and name what they form.

slides.heading: Endosperm comes first
slides.body_md: Endosperm development **precedes** embryo development. The primary endosperm cell divides repeatedly to form a **triploid endosperm** tissue, packed with reserve food for the developing embryo. Most commonly, the nucleus first divides many times **without walls** (free-nuclear endosperm); walls form later (cellular endosperm).

nodes.label: Free-nuclear endosperm: many nuclei, no walls

visual.alt: Flow of endosperm development from the primary endosperm nucleus to free-nuclear and then cellular endosperm

slides.narration: Why does the endosperm start first? Because the embryo needs a food supply ready before it grows. A tender coconut shows both stages. The coconut water is free-nuclear endosperm, made of thousands of nuclei floating in fluid. The white kernel around it is cellular endosperm.

slides.heading: Albuminous and non-albuminous seeds
slides.body_md: In some seeds the developing embryo **uses up** the endosperm completely before the seed matures; in others, part of it **persists** in the mature seed. In a few seeds, remnants of the **nucellus** also persist as the **perisperm**.

rows: Used up; food stored in cotyledons
Persists and is used during germination

visual.alt: Table of non-albuminous and albuminous seeds and seeds with perisperm, with examples

slides.narration: Split a soaked groundnut: the two big halves are cotyledons, full of stored food, and no endosperm is left. A grain of wheat is different; most of it is endosperm, which is why wheat flour is mostly starch. Black pepper and beet keep some of the old nucellus as perisperm.

slides.heading: From zygote to embryo
slides.body_md: The **zygote** lies at the **micropylar end** of the embryo sac. Most zygotes divide only after some endosperm has formed. Early stages are similar in dicots and monocots.

visual.alt: Flow of embryo development: zygote, proembryo, globular, heart-shaped and mature embryo

slides.narration: The zygote waits for the food supply to be ready, then divides to form a proembryo. This becomes a ball of cells, the globular stage, and then a heart-shaped embryo as the cotyledons begin to bulge. Finally it matures into an embryo with a clear shoot end and root end.

slides.heading: A dicot embryo
slides.body_md: A typical dicot embryo has an **embryonal axis** and **two cotyledons**. The part above the cotyledons is the **epicotyl**, ending in the **plumule** (stem tip). The part below is the **hypocotyl**, ending in the **radicle** (root tip) covered by a **root cap**.

Below them, hypo means under, so hypocotyl, ending in the radicle, the future root, protected by a root cap. A bean or gram seed shows this clearly when you split it.

slides.body_md: Monocot embryos have **one cotyledon**. In grasses it is the **scutellum**, on one side of the axis. The **plumule** and leaf primordia are enclosed in a hollow foliar sheath, the **coleoptile**; the **radicle** and root cap are enclosed in an undifferentiated sheath, the **coleorhiza**.

slides.narration: In a grass embryo, the single cotyledon is a shield-shaped scutellum that absorbs food from the endosperm. Each growing tip has its own protective sleeve: the coleoptile around the shoot and the coleorhiza around the root. Some grasses also have a small flap, the epiblast. Remember: coleoptile on top, coleorhiza at the root end.

slides.heading: Quick check: sheaths of a grass embryo
slides.body_md: Which structure encloses the radicle and root cap in a grass embryo?
slides.narration: Quick check. One sheath protects the shoot, the other protects the root. Which is which?

slides.heading: Ovule to seed
slides.body_md: The **seed** is the final product of sexual reproduction: a **fertilised ovule**. It has a **seed coat**, cotyledons and an embryonal axis. As it matures it dries to about **10–15 percent moisture** by mass, its metabolism slows down, and it may enter **dormancy**.

rows: Small pore in the seed coat: lets in oxygen and water during germination
Usually used up; perisperm in a few seeds

visual.alt: Table showing which part of the ovule becomes which part of the seed

slides.narration: Every part of the seed can be traced back to the ovule. The integuments harden into the seed coat, and the micropyle remains as a tiny pore through which water enters when the seed germinates. Drying out is essential: a dry, dormant seed can wait through a bad season and germinate only when moisture and temperature are right.

slides.heading: Ovary to fruit
slides.body_md: The **ovary** develops into the **fruit**, and the **ovary wall** becomes the **pericarp**, fleshy as in guava and orange or dry as in groundnut and mustard. In some plants the **thalamus** also forms part of the fruit, giving **false fruits**. Some fruits form **without fertilisation**: **parthenocarpy**.

rows: Banana; can be induced with growth hormones

visual.alt: Table of true, false and parthenocarpic fruits with what they develop from and examples

slides.narration: Bite into an apple and most of what you eat is swollen thalamus, not ovary, so the apple is called a false fruit. The core is the real ovary. Banana is parthenocarpic: the fruit develops without fertilisation, so it has no viable seeds. Growers can also induce seedless fruits by spraying growth hormones.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how many pollen grains and meioses?
slides.body_md: A pea pod contains 10 seeds. What is the minimum number of ovules fertilised, pollen grains, male gametes and meiotic divisions involved?
bullets: Step 1 — Each seed is one fertilised ovule: **10 ovules**.
Step 2 — One pollen tube serves one ovule and delivers both its male gametes there: **10 pollen grains**, **20 male gametes**.
Step 3 — Female side: one meiosis per ovule gives 10 meioses. Male side: one meiosis gives 4 pollen grains, so at least $\lceil 10/4 \rceil = 3$.
Total — at least **13** meiotic divisions.

visual.alt: Worked table: 10 seeds need 10 ovules, 10 pollen grains, 20 male gametes and at least 13 meioses

slides.narration: Each seed needs one ovule, one pollen grain and two male gametes, because double fertilisation uses both. So ten seeds need ten pollen grains and twenty male gametes. Meiosis is lopsided: each ovule needs its own meiosis, but one meiosis in the anther gives four pollen grains. Ten divided by four, rounded up, is three. So the minimum is thirteen meioses.

slides.heading: Why seeds matter
slides.body_md: Seeds are the basis of agriculture and of plant survival on land.

rows: Pollination and fertilisation do not need water
Seeds and fruits spread to new places
Endosperm or cotyledons feed the seedling
Hard seed coat protects the embryo
Seeds come from sexual reproduction, giving new combinations
An Arctic lupine seed germinated after about 10,000 years; a date palm seed about 2000 years old has germinated

visual.alt: Table of the advantages of seeds, including records of long seed viability

slides.narration: Seeds let plants wait. Dormant seeds can be stored for the next sowing season, which is the foundation of farming. Some seeds stay alive for astonishing times: a lupine seed from the Arctic grew after about ten thousand years, and a date palm seed around two thousand years old also germinated. Fruits help too, by protecting seeds and helping their dispersal.

slides.heading: Apomixis
slides.body_md: **Apomixis** is the formation of **seeds without fertilisation**: an asexual process that mimics sexual reproduction. It occurs in some members of the sunflower family and in grasses.

nodes.label: Diploid egg formed without meiosis develops into an embryo
Nucellus or integument cells divide, push into the embryo sac and form embryos

visual.alt: Flow of two routes of apomixis, both giving offspring genetically like the mother

slides.narration: In apomixis a seed forms, but no fertilisation takes place. Either an egg is formed without meiosis, so it is already diploid and grows into an embryo by itself, or cells of the nucellus or integuments push into the embryo sac and become embryos. Either way, the offspring are genetic copies of the mother plant.

slides.heading: Polyembryony and hybrid seeds
slides.body_md: When nucellar cells form extra embryos, a seed may hold **more than one embryo**: **polyembryony**, as in many **Citrus** and **mango** varieties. Apomixis interests the **hybrid seed industry**.

rows: Seeds from a hybrid crop show segregation, so the hybrid characters are lost
Farmers must buy new hybrid seed every year
Farmers could save and resow their own hybrid seed
Hybrid seed is costly to produce
Hybrid seed could be multiplied cheaply

visual.alt: Table of problems with hybrid seeds and how apomictic hybrids could solve them

slides.narration: Squeeze the seed of an orange or a mango and you may find several seedlings coming out of one seed; that is polyembryony. Now think of a farmer growing a high-yielding hybrid. If she sows seeds from her crop, the characters segregate and the yield falls. If scientists could make hybrids apomictic, she could save her own seed year after year.

slides.heading: Quick check: seed without fertilisation
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about apomixis and parthenocarpy.
slides.narration: Quick check. One process makes a seed without fertilisation, the other makes a fruit without fertilisation. Read carefully.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Double fertilisation: **syngamy** (gamete + egg → diploid zygote) and **triple fusion** (gamete + 2 polar nuclei → triploid primary endosperm nucleus).
Endosperm develops before the embryo; free-nuclear then cellular (coconut water and kernel).
Non-albuminous seeds (pea, groundnut) vs albuminous seeds (wheat, maize, castor); perisperm in black pepper and beet.
Dicot embryo: plumule, epicotyl, cotyledons, hypocotyl, radicle, root cap. Grass embryo: scutellum, coleoptile, coleorhiza, epiblast.
Ovule → seed (integuments → seed coat); ovary → fruit (wall → pericarp); false fruits include thalamus.
**Apomixis**: seed without fertilisation; **polyembryony**: many embryos in a seed; **parthenocarpy**: fruit without fertilisation.

visual.alt: Summary table of double fertilisation, apomixis and parthenocarpy

slides.narration: To recap. Two male gametes, two fusions: a diploid zygote and a triploid endosperm. Endosperm grows first and feeds the embryo. The ovule becomes the seed and the ovary becomes the fruit. And apomixis, polyembryony and parthenocarpy are special cases that break the usual rules, with real uses in agriculture.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Name both fusions in double fertilisation and give the **ploidy** of each product.
The seed coat and pericarp are **maternal, diploid** tissue, not products of fertilisation.
Coconut: water = **free-nuclear** endosperm; kernel = **cellular** endosperm.
Do not mix up **apomixis** (seed, no fertilisation) and **parthenocarpy** (fruit, no seed).
In counting questions, both male gametes of one pollen tube are used in **one** ovule.
slides.narration: Final tips. Give the ploidy every time you mention syngamy or triple fusion. Remember that the seed coat and fruit wall belong to the mother plant. Keep apomixis and parthenocarpy apart: one gives a seed without fertilisation, the other a fruit without seeds. And in counting questions, one pollen grain serves one ovule.

notes.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Stamen, anther and microsporogenesis
sections.body_md:
The flower is the reproductive organ of flowering plants (angiosperms). Hormonal and structural changes turn a shoot apex into a floral bud, in which the **androecium** (stamens) and **gynoecium** (pistils) develop.

A **stamen** has a **filament** and an **anther**. A typical anther is **bilobed** and **dithecous** (two thecae per lobe), with **four microsporangia** at its corners that later become **pollen sacs**.

**Wall of a microsporangium (outside → inside):** epidermis, endothecium, middle layers (these three protect and help dehiscence) and **tapetum**, which nourishes the developing pollen; tapetal cells have dense cytoplasm and often more than one nucleus.

**Microsporogenesis:** cells of the **sporogenous tissue** act as **microspore (pollen) mother cells** (diploid). Each undergoes **meiosis** to form a **microspore tetrad** of four haploid cells. As the anther matures and dehydrates, the microspores separate and develop into **pollen grains**. One meiosis → four pollen grains.

Innermost wall layer of the microsporangium; nourishes the developing pollen.
Formation of microspores from a microspore mother cell by meiosis.

sections.heading: 2. The pollen grain (male gametophyte)
sections.body_md:
Pollen grains are usually spherical, about 25–50 micrometres in diameter, with a two-layered wall.

- **Exine:** hard outer layer of **sporopollenin**, one of the most resistant organic materials; it withstands high temperatures and strong acids and alkalis, and no known enzyme degrades it, so pollen is well preserved as fossils. **Germ pores** are gaps where sporopollenin is absent.
- **Intine:** thin, continuous inner layer of **cellulose and pectin**.

A mature pollen grain contains a large **vegetative cell** (abundant food reserve, large irregular nucleus) and a small, spindle-shaped **generative cell** floating in its cytoplasm. In over 60 percent of angiosperms, pollen is shed at this **two-celled** stage; in the rest, the generative cell divides by mitosis into **two male gametes** before shedding (**three-celled** stage).

**Pollen and people:** pollen of many plants (for example Parthenium, carrot grass) causes allergies such as asthma and bronchitis; pollen is used as a food supplement; viability ranges from about 30 minutes (rice, wheat) to months (some members of the rose, pea and potato families); pollen can be stored for years in **liquid nitrogen (about −196 °C)** in pollen banks for breeding.

Region of the exine without sporopollenin, through which the pollen tube emerges.

sections.heading: 3. Pistil, ovule and the embryo sac
sections.body_md:
The **gynoecium** may be **monocarpellary** (one pistil) or **multicarpellary** (many); pistils may be **syncarpous** (fused, as in poppy) or **apocarpous** (free, as in Michelia). Each pistil has a **stigma**, a **style** and an **ovary**; ovules arise from the **placenta** in the ovarian cavity.

**Ovule (megasporangium):** attached to the placenta by the **funicle**; the junction with the ovule body is the **hilum**. One or two **integuments** enclose it except at the **micropyle**; the opposite, basal end is the **chalaza**. Inside the integuments is the **nucellus**, which holds the **embryo sac** (female gametophyte). An ovule usually has one embryo sac.

**Megasporogenesis:** a single **megaspore mother cell** differentiates in the micropylar region of the nucellus and undergoes **meiosis** to form **four megaspores**. In most flowering plants one is **functional** and three degenerate; the embryo sac formed from one megaspore is **monosporic**.

**Embryo sac development:** the functional megaspore nucleus divides by mitosis three times, free-nuclear, giving 2, 4 and then 8 nuclei (four at each pole). Six nuclei are walled off into cells; one nucleus from each pole moves to the centre as a **polar nucleus**. The mature embryo sac is **7-celled and 8-nucleate**:
- micropylar end: **egg apparatus** = egg cell + two **synergids** (with the **filiform apparatus**, which guides the pollen tube);
- chalazal end: three **antipodal** cells;
- centre: large **central cell** with two polar nuclei.

key_terms.definition_md: Formation of megaspores from the megaspore mother cell by meiosis.
Formation of the embryo sac from a single functional megaspore.
Finger-like thickenings at the micropylar tip of the synergids that guide the pollen tube.

sections.heading: 4. Pollination: kinds and agents
sections.body_md:
**Pollination** is the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma.

| Kind | Pollen from | Genetically |
|---|---|---|
| Autogamy | Same flower | Self |
| Geitonogamy | Another flower of the same plant (needs an agent) | Self |
| Xenogamy | A flower of a different plant | Cross: new gene combinations |

**Chasmogamous** flowers open and expose anthers and stigma; **cleistogamous** flowers never open and are always autogamous, giving **assured seed set** even without pollinators (Viola, Oxalis, Commelina have both kinds).

**Wind:** light, non-sticky pollen; well-exposed stamens; large, often feathery stigma; usually a single ovule per ovary; many flowers in an inflorescence (maize tassels shed pollen; the silks of the cob are stigmas and styles). Common in grasses.

**Water:** about 30 genera, mostly monocots: **Vallisneria** (female flowers reach the surface on long stalks; male flowers or pollen float to them), **Hydrilla**, seagrasses such as **Zostera** (long ribbon-like pollen carried under water). Pollen is protected by a **mucilaginous covering**. Water hyacinth and water lily, though aquatic, are pollinated by insects or wind.

**Animals:** bees are the dominant biotic agents; others include butterflies, flies, beetles, wasps, moths, sunbirds, hummingbirds and bats. Flowers are large, colourful, fragrant and rich in nectar, or small and clustered; fly- and beetle-pollinated flowers may smell foul. Rewards are **nectar and pollen**, or a **safe place to lay eggs** (Amorphophallus). **Yucca and its moth** depend on each other: the moth lays eggs in the ovary and its larvae eat some seeds. Pollen and nectar **robbers** take rewards without pollinating.

key_terms.definition_md: Transfer of pollen to another flower of the same plant; functionally cross but genetically self-pollination.
Transfer of pollen to the stigma of a flower on a different plant.
A flower that never opens and is always self-pollinated.

sections.heading: 5. Outbreeding devices, pollen–pistil interaction and hybridisation
sections.body_md:
Continued self-pollination leads to **inbreeding depression**. **Outbreeding devices**:
1. Pollen release and stigma receptivity **not synchronised**.
2. Anther and stigma at **different positions**.
3. **Self-incompatibility:** a genetic mechanism that prevents pollen of the same flower or plant from germinating or growing in the pistil.
4. **Unisexual flowers:** **monoecious** plants (castor, maize) prevent autogamy but **not** geitonogamy; **dioecious** plants (papaya) prevent **both**.

**Pollen–pistil interaction:** the pistil recognises compatible pollen through chemical components of the pollen and pistil, and promotes it; incompatible pollen is inhibited at germination or tube growth. Compatible pollen germinates through a **germ pore**; the **pollen tube** grows through the stigma and style into the ovary (a two-celled pollen grain's generative cell divides in the tube), enters the ovule through the **micropyle**, and is guided by the **filiform apparatus** into a **synergid**.

**Artificial hybridisation:** ensures only the desired pollen reaches the stigma.
- **Emasculation:** removal of anthers from a bisexual flower bud before dehiscence (not needed for female flowers of unisexual plants).
- **Bagging:** covering the flower with a butter-paper bag to keep out unwanted pollen; when the stigma is receptive, it is dusted with the chosen pollen and **rebagged**.

key_terms.definition_md: Genetic mechanism that stops pollen from fertilising ovules of the same flower or plant.
Removal of anthers from a bisexual flower bud before they dehisce.
Covering an emasculated or female flower with a bag to prevent contamination by unwanted pollen.

sections.heading: 6. Double fertilisation, endosperm and embryo
sections.body_md:
The pollen tube releases **two male gametes** into a synergid.
- **Syngamy:** male gamete + egg → **zygote (2n)**.
- **Triple fusion:** male gamete + two polar nuclei → **primary endosperm nucleus (3n)**; the central cell becomes the **primary endosperm cell**.

Two fusions in one embryo sac = **double fertilisation**, a feature of flowering plants.

**Endosperm** develops **before** the embryo. The primary endosperm cell divides repeatedly to form triploid endosperm with reserve food. Commonly it is first **free-nuclear** and later becomes **cellular**: in coconut, the water is free-nuclear endosperm (thousands of nuclei) and the white kernel is cellular endosperm. The endosperm may be consumed completely before seed maturity (**non-albuminous** seeds: pea, groundnut, beans) or persist (**albuminous** seeds: wheat, maize, barley, castor, coconut). Persistent nucellus is **perisperm** (black pepper, beet).

**Embryo:** the zygote, at the micropylar end, divides after some endosperm forms: proembryo → globular → heart-shaped → mature embryo.
- **Dicot:** embryonal axis + two cotyledons; **epicotyl** (above cotyledons) ends in the **plumule**; **hypocotyl** (below) ends in the **radicle** with a **root cap**.
- **Monocot (grass):** one cotyledon, the **scutellum**, lateral; **coleoptile** encloses the shoot apex and leaf primordia; **coleorhiza** encloses the radicle and root cap; an **epiblast** may be present.

key_terms.definition_md: Fusion of a male gamete with the two polar nuclei, forming the triploid primary endosperm nucleus.
Persistent remains of the nucellus in some seeds, such as black pepper and beet.
The single, shield-shaped cotyledon of a grass embryo.

sections.heading: 7. Seed and fruit
sections.body_md:
The **seed** is a fertilised ovule. **Integuments → seed coat**; the **micropyle** remains as a pore that lets oxygen and water in during germination. Mature seeds dry to about **10–15 percent moisture** by mass; metabolism slows and the embryo may become **dormant** until conditions are favourable.

The **ovary → fruit** and the **ovary wall → pericarp** (fleshy, as in guava and orange, or dry, as in groundnut and mustard). In **false fruits** the **thalamus** also contributes (apple, strawberry, cashew). **Parthenocarpic** fruits develop **without fertilisation** and are seedless (banana); they can be induced with growth hormones.

**Advantages of seeds:** pollination and fertilisation are free of water; seeds are dispersed widely and colonise new areas; stored food nourishes the seedling; the hard seed coat protects the embryo; seeds of sexual reproduction carry **variation**; dormancy lets them be stored, which is the basis of agriculture. Some seeds stay viable for very long: an Arctic lupine seed germinated after about **10,000 years**, and a date palm seed about **2000 years** old has germinated.

key_terms.definition_md: Wall of the fruit, developed from the ovary wall.
A fruit in which the thalamus also contributes to the fleshy part, such as apple.
Development of a fruit without fertilisation; the fruit is seedless.

sections.heading: 8. Apomixis and polyembryony
sections.body_md:
**Apomixis:** formation of **seeds without fertilisation**, a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction (some members of the sunflower family, grasses).
- A **diploid egg** forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation; or
- cells of the **nucellus** (or integuments) divide, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.

**Polyembryony:** more than one embryo in a seed, often from nucellar cells, as in many **Citrus** and **mango** varieties.

**Importance:** hybrid seeds give high yields, but progeny of hybrids **segregate**, so farmers must buy fresh hybrid seed every year. If hybrids were made **apomictic**, there would be no segregation, and farmers could keep using their own hybrid seed. Scientists are trying to identify the genes for apomixis and transfer them into hybrid varieties.

key_terms.definition_md: Formation of seeds without fertilisation.
Occurrence of more than one embryo in a seed.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that the embryo sac has eight cells: it has **seven cells and eight nuclei**.
- Calling geitonogamy cross-pollination without adding that it is genetically self-pollination.
- Saying monoecious plants prevent geitonogamy (only dioecious plants do).
- Giving the endosperm as diploid: it is **triploid** (in typical flowering plants).
- Treating the seed coat or pericarp as products of fertilisation; they are maternal tissue.
- Mixing up apomixis (seed without fertilisation) and parthenocarpy (fruit without fertilisation).
- Naming water hyacinth or water lily as water-pollinated.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, term, ploidy or example.
- 2–3-mark answers: term or name (1) + process or reason (1) + example, comparison point or labelled sketch (1).
- 5-mark answers: labelled diagram (embryo sac, anther, ovule, embryo) (2) + process in the correct order (2) + significance or one more point (1).
- Case-based items: two 1-mark parts from the passage and a 2-mark part with an internal choice, often reading data or applying a counting rule.

questions.stem_md: A microspore tetrad is formed when a microspore mother cell divides. Which division forms it, and what is the ploidy of each microspore?

options.text_md: Mitosis; each microspore is diploid.
Meiosis; each microspore is diploid.
Mitosis; each microspore is haploid.
Meiosis; each microspore is haploid.

questions.solution_md: The diploid mother cell undergoes meiosis, so the four microspores of the tetrad are haploid — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a mutant plant, the innermost wall layer of the microsporangium breaks down very early, before the microspores have formed walls. Which outcome is most likely?

options.text_md: Pollen grains fail to develop properly, because this layer nourishes them.
The anther cannot split open, because this layer causes dehiscence.
Ovules fail to form, because this layer supplies the ovary.
Pollen grains become diploid, because meiosis is skipped.

questions.solution_md: The innermost layer is the tapetum, which nourishes the developing pollen; without it, pollen development fails — option (a). Dehiscence depends on the outer layers (b); the tapetum has nothing to do with ovules (c) or with meiosis (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Pollen grains are well preserved as fossils.

**Reason (R):** The exine of pollen contains sporopollenin, which withstands high temperatures, strong acids and alkalis, and is not broken down by any known enzyme.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the resistance of sporopollenin is exactly why pollen survives for long periods as fossils — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A typical mature embryo sac of a flowering plant has

options.text_md: 8 cells and 8 nuclei
7 cells and 7 nuclei
7 cells and 8 nuclei
8 cells and 7 nuclei

questions.solution_md: Three antipodals + egg + two synergids + one central cell = 7 cells; the central cell has two polar nuclei, so there are 8 nuclei — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A plant has 20 chromosomes in its root tip cells. How many chromosomes are present in a synergid and in a nucellus cell of this plant?

options.text_md: 20 and 20
10 and 10
10 and 20
20 and 30

questions.solution_md: Root cells are diploid, $2n = 20$. A synergid is a cell of the embryo sac, formed by mitosis from the haploid megaspore: 10. The nucellus is sporophyte tissue: 20 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Through which part of the pollen wall does the pollen tube emerge?

options.text_md: The thickest part of the exine
A germ pore, where sporopollenin is absent
The generative cell wall
Any point, as the exine dissolves on the stigma

questions.solution_md: Germ pores are the gaps in the exine without sporopollenin; the intine bulges out through one of them as the pollen tube — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In more than 60 percent of flowering plants, pollen grains are shed at the

options.text_md: three-celled stage: a vegetative cell and two male gametes
one-celled stage: a single microspore
tetrad stage: four microspores held together
two-celled stage: a vegetative cell and a generative cell

questions.solution_md: Most flowering plants shed two-celled pollen; the generative cell divides later, in the pollen tube — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The nucellus of an ovule is a haploid tissue, like the embryo sac it encloses.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. The nucellus is part of the parent plant (sporophyte) and is diploid; only the embryo sac, formed from a meiotic megaspore, is haploid.

questions.stem_md: A breeder wants to pollinate rice plants at one research farm with pollen collected from a rice variety growing at another farm, three hours away by road. What should she do to make the cross succeed?

options.text_md: Store the collected pollen in liquid nitrogen and carry it in that state.
Carry the pollen in an open paper envelope so that it stays dry.
Soak the pollen in water so that it does not dry out.
Nothing special, as rice pollen stays viable for several months.

questions.solution_md: Rice pollen loses viability within about half an hour of release, so it must be kept alive by cryopreservation in liquid nitrogen (about −196 °C) — option (a). (d) is true only of some other families; soaking (c) would ruin the pollen.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Each polar nucleus of the embryo sac is haploid.

**Reason (R):** The polar nuclei are formed by meiosis of the functional megaspore nucleus inside the embryo sac.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: each polar nucleus is haploid. R is false: meiosis happens once, in the megaspore mother cell; the functional megaspore nucleus then divides only by mitosis, which keeps the haploid number — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Each microsporangium of an anther contains 30 microspore mother cells. If the anther has the usual number of microsporangia and every mother cell completes meiosis, how many pollen grains will it produce?
questions.solution_md: A typical anther has 4 microsporangia. Mother cells $= 4 \times 30 = 120$; each gives 4 pollen grains, so pollen $= 120 \times 4 = 480$.

questions.stem_md: How many successive free-nuclear mitotic divisions of the functional megaspore nucleus are needed to produce the 8 nuclei of a typical embryo sac?
questions.solution_md: Each mitosis doubles the nuclei: $1 \to 2 \to 4 \to 8$. Since $2^k = 8$, the number of divisions is $k = \log_2 8 = 3$.

questions.stem_md: Match each part of the ovule (column I) with its description (column II).

options.text_md: Funicle
Micropyle
Chalaza
Nucellus

match_right.text_md: Small opening left by the integuments
Mass of cells inside the integuments that holds the embryo sac
Stalk that attaches the ovule to the placenta
Basal part of the ovule, opposite the micropylar end

questions.solution_md: Funicle = stalk to the placenta; micropyle = opening between the integuments; chalaza = base opposite the micropyle; nucellus = tissue containing the embryo sac.

questions.stem_md: The innermost wall layer of a microsporangium, which nourishes the developing pollen grains, is the ______.
questions.solution_md: Tapetum.

questions.stem_md: The generative cell of a pollen grain divides by ______ to form two male gametes.
questions.solution_md: Mitosis: the generative cell is already haploid, so the two male gametes are haploid too.

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between microsporogenesis and megasporogenesis.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Site:** microsporogenesis occurs in the microsporangium of the anther; megasporogenesis occurs in the nucellus of the ovule.

2. **Number of mother cells:** many microspore mother cells form in each microsporangium; usually a single megaspore mother cell forms in an ovule.

3. **Fate of the four spores:** all four microspores of a tetrad develop into pollen grains; usually only one megaspore is functional and the other three degenerate.

questions.solution_md: Compare the site, the number of mother cells and the fate of the four products of meiosis.

marking_scheme.step: Difference in number of mother cells
Difference in how many spores survive

questions.stem_md: Describe the formation of the female gametophyte of a flowering plant, starting from the megaspore mother cell. Draw a labelled diagram of the mature embryo sac.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Megasporogenesis.** A single, large megaspore mother cell with dense cytoplasm differentiates in the micropylar region of the nucellus. It undergoes meiosis to form four haploid megaspores. Usually three degenerate and one remains functional (monosporic development).

**Embryo sac formation.** The nucleus of the functional megaspore divides by mitosis three times without wall formation (free-nuclear), giving 2, 4 and then 8 nuclei, four at each pole. Six nuclei become enclosed in cells; one nucleus from each pole moves to the centre as a polar nucleus.

**Mature embryo sac (diagram).** It is 7-celled and 8-nucleate: at the micropylar end, the egg apparatus of one egg cell and two synergids with a filiform apparatus; at the chalazal end, three antipodal cells; in the centre, a large central cell with two polar nuclei.

questions.solution_md: Order: meiosis of the megaspore mother cell → one functional megaspore → three free-nuclear mitoses → wall formation → seven-celled, eight-nucleate embryo sac.

marking_scheme.step: Megaspore mother cell, meiosis, four megaspores, one functional
Three free-nuclear mitoses giving eight nuclei
Wall formation and the movement of polar nuclei
Labelled diagram: egg apparatus, antipodals, central cell with polar nuclei, filiform apparatus

questions.stem_md: In a hybrid plant, the anthers look normal but contain only shrunken, empty pollen grains. Microscopy shows that the innermost layer of the anther wall is abnormal. Name this layer and explain how its defect could cause the observation.

answer.model_answer_md: The layer is the **tapetum**. It nourishes the developing microspores and pollen grains; if it is defective, the pollen does not receive the food and materials it needs to develop, so the grains remain shrunken and empty (male sterile).

questions.solution_md: Identify the innermost wall layer and link its nourishing role to pollen development.

marking_scheme.step: Explains that it nourishes developing pollen, so pollen fails to develop

questions.stem_md: Pollen grains of plants that lived millions of years ago are still found in rocks and lake sediments. Explain why, and state where the pollen wall is weakest.

answer.model_answer_md: The exine is made of **sporopollenin**, which resists high temperature, strong acids and alkalis and is not degraded by any known enzyme, so pollen survives for millions of years as fossils. The wall is weakest at the **germ pores**, where sporopollenin is absent.

questions.solution_md: Link the chemical resistance of sporopollenin to fossilisation, and recall germ pores.

marking_scheme.step: Sporopollenin in the exine is highly resistant

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination but genetically similar to autogamy.

**Reason (R):** In geitonogamy, an agent carries pollen from one flower to another flower of the same plant.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. An agent moves pollen between two flowers (functionally cross), but both flowers belong to the same plant, so the pollen is genetically the same (like autogamy). R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which set of features best fits a wind-pollinated flower?

options.text_md: Bright petals; strong scent; plenty of nectar
Sticky pollen; hidden stamens; small smooth stigma
Light, non-sticky pollen; exposed stamens; large feathery stigma
Pollen with a mucilage coat; flowers on long stalks reaching the water surface

questions.solution_md: Wind flowers need pollen that air can carry and stigmas that can catch it — option (c). (a) fits insect pollination, (d) water pollination, and (b) would prevent wind pollination.

questions.stem_md: Through which opening does a pollen tube usually enter the ovule?

options.text_md: Chalaza
Micropyle
Hilum
Germ pore

questions.solution_md: The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and then a synergid — option (b). A germ pore (d) is in the pollen wall, not the ovule.

questions.stem_md: Commelina produces some flowers that never open. Which statement about the seeds formed in these flowers is correct?

options.text_md: They form only if insects carry pollen from other plants.
They show more variation than seeds from open flowers.
They are formed without fertilisation, by apomixis.
Seed set is assured even if no pollinator visits, but the offspring show little variation.

questions.solution_md: Cleistogamous flowers are always autogamous: their own pollen reaches their own stigma inside the closed flower, so seed set is assured but there is little variation — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A family plants a single papaya seedling in their garden. Years later it flowers every season but never forms fruit, although bees visit the flowers. What is the most likely reason?

options.text_md: Papaya is monoecious, so its flowers cannot be pollinated by bees.
Papaya is dioecious; the plant is female (or male) and there is no plant of the other sex nearby.
Papaya flowers are cleistogamous, so bees cannot reach the stigma.
Papaya pollen is shed only after the stigma has dried, on every plant.

questions.solution_md: Papaya has male and female flowers on separate plants (dioecy). With only one plant, no pollen of the other sex is available, so no fertilisation or fruit occurs — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which of these aquatic plants is pollinated by water?

options.text_md: Water hyacinth
Water lily
Vallisneria
Lotus

questions.solution_md: Vallisneria is pollinated by water; water hyacinth and water lily, though aquatic, are pollinated by insects or wind, as is lotus — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? All plants that grow in water are pollinated by water.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Most aquatic plants with flowers above the water, such as water hyacinth and water lily, are pollinated by insects or wind; water pollination is limited to about 30 genera, such as Vallisneria and Zostera.

questions.stem_md: Suppose the only moth species that visits a Yucca species in a region dies out. What would most likely happen to that Yucca?

options.text_md: It would fail to set seed, because this moth is its only pollinator.
It would set more seed, because no larvae would eat the seeds.
It would switch to wind pollination in the next generation.
Nothing, because Yucca is pollinated by water.

questions.solution_md: Yucca and its moth depend on each other: only the moth pollinates the flower. Without it, there is no pollination, so no seeds — option (a). Plants do not switch pollinators within a generation (c).

questions.stem_md: In which of these crosses can the breeder skip emasculation and only bag the flower?

questions.stem_md: Continued self-pollination can lead to inbreeding depression. Describe three devices by which flowering plants discourage self-pollination.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Timing:** pollen is released when the stigma of the same flower is not receptive (before or after it), so self-pollen cannot fertilise.

2. **Position:** anthers and stigma are placed apart in the flower, so pollen does not reach its own stigma.

3. **Self-incompatibility:** a genetic mechanism lets the pistil recognise pollen from the same flower or plant and stop its germination or pollen-tube growth. (Unisexual flowers are another device.)

questions.solution_md: Any three of: timing, position, self-incompatibility, unisexual flowers (monoecy, dioecy).

Second device with how it works
Third device with how it works

questions.stem_md: In a maize field, tassels at the top of the plant shed dry, powdery pollen, and long silky threads hang out of the young cobs lower down. Explain how three features of maize suit it to wind pollination.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Light, non-sticky pollen** produced in large amounts is easily carried by air currents.

2. **Exposed male flowers** in the tassel at the top of the plant release pollen into the wind.

3. **Long, feathery silks** (the styles and stigmas) hang out of the cob and give a large surface to trap airborne pollen; each ovary has a single ovule, so one pollen grain is enough for each grain of the cob.

questions.stem_md: A breeder wants to cross a wheat variety A, which has bisexual flowers and high yield, as the female parent, with variety B, which resists a rust disease, as the male parent. (a) Describe, with reasons, the steps she must follow. (b) What would go wrong if she skipped the first step? (c) Why would she not need this first step if variety A bore only unisexual female flowers?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Emasculation:** before the anthers of A dehisce, she removes them from the flower bud with forceps, so A cannot pollinate itself. **Bagging:** she covers the emasculated flower with a butter-paper bag to keep out unwanted pollen. When the stigma becomes **receptive**, she dusts it with pollen collected from B and **rebags** it so the fruit and seeds develop free of contamination.

(b) The anthers of A would shed pollen on its own stigma (autogamy is common in wheat), so many seeds would come from self-pollination and would not carry B’s rust resistance.

(c) A female flower has no anthers, so there is no self-pollen to remove; bagging before the flower opens is enough.

questions.solution_md: Emasculation, bagging, dusting at receptivity, rebagging; then the consequence of self-pollen and the case of unisexual flowers.

marking_scheme.step: Dusting chosen pollen at receptivity and rebagging
(b) Self-pollination gives seeds without the desired trait
(c) Female flowers have no anthers, so only bagging

questions.stem_md: Describe the events from the moment a compatible pollen grain lands on the stigma until the male gametes are released in the embryo sac. Why is the pistil’s ability to recognise pollen important?

answer.model_answer_md:
**Recognition.** The pistil identifies whether the pollen is of the right type through chemical components of the pollen and the pistil. Compatible pollen is accepted and promoted; incompatible pollen, of another species or the same plant in self-incompatible species, is inhibited.

**Germination and tube growth.** The compatible pollen grain germinates and a pollen tube grows out through a germ pore. The contents of the pollen grain move into the tube, which grows through the tissues of the stigma and style and reaches the ovary. In two-celled pollen, the generative cell divides in the tube to form two male gametes.

**Entry.** The tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and then enters one of the synergids, guided by the filiform apparatus, where it releases the two male gametes.

**Importance.** Recognition makes sure that only suitable pollen of the same species, often from another plant, fertilises the ovules; this prevents wasted ovules and helps avoid inbreeding.

questions.solution_md: Recognition → germination through a germ pore → tube through stigma and style → micropyle → synergid via the filiform apparatus; importance of recognition.

marking_scheme.step: Germination through a germ pore and growth through stigma and style
Formation of male gametes (in tube or before shedding)
Entry through the micropyle into a synergid guided by the filiform apparatus
