questions.stem_md: What is meant by double fertilisation? Name the two fusions and give the ploidy of each product.

answer.model_answer_md:
Double fertilisation is the occurrence of **two fusions in the same embryo sac**, using the two male gametes from one pollen tube.

1. **Syngamy:** one male gamete fuses with the egg cell, forming the **diploid zygote**, which develops into the embryo.

2. **Triple fusion:** the other male gamete fuses with the two polar nuclei, forming the **triploid primary endosperm nucleus**; the central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell and develops into the endosperm.

questions.solution_md: Define double fertilisation, then give syngamy (2n) and triple fusion (3n).

marking_scheme.step: Definition: two fusions in one embryo sac
Triple fusion → triploid primary endosperm nucleus

questions.stem_md: In most flowering plants, the zygote divides only after some endosperm has formed. Explain why this sequence is useful, using coconut as an example of developing endosperm.

answer.model_answer_md: The endosperm stores **food for the developing embryo**, so forming it first ensures nourishment is ready when the embryo grows. In coconut, the primary endosperm nucleus divides many times to give **free-nuclear** endosperm (coconut water), which later becomes **cellular** (the white kernel).

questions.solution_md: Food supply first; coconut water (free-nuclear) and kernel (cellular).

marking_scheme.step: Endosperm nourishes the embryo, so it must be ready first

questions.stem_md: Give three differences between the embryo of a bean seed (dicot) and that of a maize grain (monocot).

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Cotyledons:** the bean embryo has two cotyledons; the maize embryo has one, the shield-shaped scutellum, on one side of the axis.

2. **Shoot sheath:** the plumule of the bean has no sheath; in maize the shoot apex and leaf primordia are enclosed in a hollow foliar sheath, the coleoptile.

3. **Root sheath:** the radicle of the bean is covered only by a root cap; in maize the radicle and root cap are enclosed in a sheath, the coleorhiza.

questions.solution_md: Compare cotyledon number and position, and the coleoptile and coleorhiza.

questions.stem_md: A flowering plant has 16 chromosomes in its leaf cells. State the number of chromosomes in (a) a male gamete, (b) the zygote, (c) an endosperm cell, (d) a cell of the seed coat, (e) an antipodal cell and (f) a cell of the fruit wall. Give a reason for (c) and (d).

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 8; (b) 16; (c) 24; (d) 16; (e) 8; (f) 16.

Reason for (c): the endosperm develops from the primary endosperm nucleus formed by fusion of a male gamete with two polar nuclei, each haploid, so it is triploid.

Reason for (d): the seed coat develops from the integuments of the mother plant, which are diploid sporophyte tissue.

questions.solution_md: $2n = 16$, $n = 8$; gametes and embryo sac cells n, zygote 2n, endosperm 3n, maternal tissues 2n.

marking_scheme.step: (c) and (f) correct, with the reason for (c)

questions.stem_md: Explain double fertilisation in flowering plants with the help of a labelled diagram of the embryo sac after the entry of the pollen tube. Trace what each product develops into.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Entry.** The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle and enters one of the synergids, guided by the filiform apparatus. It releases two male gametes into the cytoplasm of the synergid.

**Syngamy.** One male gamete moves towards the egg cell and fuses with its nucleus, forming a diploid zygote.

**Triple fusion.** The other male gamete moves to the central cell and fuses with the two polar nuclei, forming a triploid primary endosperm nucleus; the central cell becomes the primary endosperm cell.

Two fusions take place in the same embryo sac, so the process is called double fertilisation.

**Products.** The primary endosperm cell develops into the endosperm, which nourishes the embryo; the zygote develops into the embryo.

**Diagram labels:** pollen tube, synergid, two male gametes, egg, polar nuclei, antipodals, micropyle.

questions.solution_md: Tube enters a synergid → two male gametes → syngamy (2n zygote) and triple fusion (3n primary endosperm nucleus) → embryo and endosperm.

marking_scheme.step: Pollen tube enters a synergid and releases two male gametes
Triple fusion forming the triploid primary endosperm nucleus
Fate: zygote → embryo, primary endosperm cell → endosperm

questions.stem_md: A bean pod contains 14 seeds. What is the minimum number of meiotic divisions (in anthers and ovules together) needed to produce them?

questions.stem_md: Why do farmers who grow high-yielding hybrid varieties usually buy fresh hybrid seed every year instead of sowing seed from their own crop?

options.text_md: In the progeny of a hybrid, the characters segregate, so the hybrid qualities are not maintained.

Hybrid plants are always parthenocarpic and give seedless fruit.

questions.stem_md: When an apple is cut across, its seeds lie in a papery central core, and the core is surrounded by thick, juicy flesh. What does this show about the apple?

The core is the ovary; most of the flesh comes from the thalamus, so the apple is a false fruit.
The flesh is endosperm that grew outside the seeds.
The core is the thalamus and the flesh is the pericarp, so the apple is parthenocarpic.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.stem_md: A grower sprays growth hormones on the flowers of a crop and obtains seedless fruits. Name the phenomenon and explain why it is not an example of apomixis.

answer.model_answer_md: This is **parthenocarpy**: the ovary develops into a fruit without fertilisation. It is not apomixis, because apomixis produces **seeds** without fertilisation, whereas parthenocarpic fruits have **no seeds** at all.

questions.solution_md: Parthenocarpy is fruit without fertilisation; apomixis is seed without fertilisation.

marking_scheme.step: Apomixis gives seeds; here no seeds form

questions.stem_md: What is apomixis? Describe two ways in which an apomictic embryo can arise, and state one reason why apomixis interests the hybrid seed industry.

answer.model_answer_md:
Apomixis is the production of **seeds without fertilisation**; it is a form of asexual reproduction that mimics sexual reproduction.

1. A **diploid egg cell** forms without reduction division and develops into an embryo without fertilisation.

2. Cells of the **nucellus** surrounding the embryo sac divide, protrude into the embryo sac and develop into embryos.

If hybrids were made apomictic, their seeds would **not segregate**, so farmers could save and resow hybrid seed every year.

questions.solution_md: Definition; diploid egg route and nucellar route; no segregation in apomictic hybrids.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the ability of seeds to dry out and become dormant has been important for agriculture.

answer.model_answer_md: Dry, dormant seeds can be **stored** safely from one harvest to the next sowing season, providing food and planting material. Dormancy also lets seeds **survive unfavourable seasons** and germinate when moisture and temperature are suitable, so crops can be sown at the right time.

questions.solution_md: Storage between seasons; survival through unfavourable conditions.

marking_scheme.step: Seeds can be stored for later sowing or food
Seeds survive unfavourable conditions and germinate later

questions.stem_md: Describe the changes that take place in the ovule and the ovary after fertilisation. Explain, with one example each, what is meant by a false fruit and a parthenocarpic fruit.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Ovule → seed.** The zygote develops into the embryo, and the primary endosperm cell into the endosperm, which may be used up (pea, groundnut) or persist (wheat, castor). The integuments harden into the seed coat; the micropyle remains as a small pore for water and oxygen during germination. The seed dries to about 10–15 percent moisture, its metabolism slows, and it may become dormant.

**Ovary → fruit.** The ovary enlarges into the fruit, and the ovary wall becomes the pericarp, which may be fleshy (guava, orange) or dry (groundnut, mustard).

**False fruit.** Here the thalamus also contributes to the fruit, as in apple, where the fleshy part is mostly thalamus.

**Parthenocarpic fruit.** This develops without fertilisation and is seedless, as in banana; such fruits can be induced with growth hormones.

questions.solution_md: Ovule parts → seed parts; ovary → fruit, wall → pericarp; false fruit (apple), parthenocarpy (banana).

marking_scheme.step: Integuments → seed coat; drying and dormancy

questions.stem_md: A seed company announces that it has produced an apomictic version of its best hybrid rice. Evaluate this claim for farmers: explain how apomixis works, why it would change the way farmers obtain seed, and one possible drawback of growing only apomictic hybrids over a large area.

answer.model_answer_md:
**How it works.** In apomixis, seeds form without fertilisation: either a diploid egg forms without meiosis and develops into an embryo, or cells of the nucellus grow into the embryo sac and form embryos. The embryo therefore has the same genes as the mother plant.

**Effect for farmers.** Seeds from an ordinary hybrid come from sexual reproduction, so characters segregate and the next crop is uneven and lower-yielding; farmers must buy new hybrid seed every season. An apomictic hybrid would breed true, so farmers could save their own seed year after year and still get hybrid yields, lowering their costs.

**Drawback.** Every plant would be genetically identical to the mother, so the crop over a large area would lack variation; a new disease or pest able to attack one plant could damage the whole crop.

**Verdict.** The claim, if true, is very useful, but farmers should keep some varietal diversity.

questions.solution_md: Mechanism of apomixis → no segregation → seed saving; drawback: uniformity and lack of variation.

marking_scheme.step: Apomictic hybrid breeds true; farmers can reuse seed
Drawback: no variation, risk from disease

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A student studied stained sections of ovules of a plant whose leaf cells have 16 chromosomes. She sorted what she saw into four stages:

| Stage | What was seen in the nucellus |
|---|---|
| I | One large cell with dense cytoplasm near the micropylar end |
| II | A row of four cells; three of them shrinking |
| III | One enlarged cell containing two nuclei, one at each end |
| IV | A sac with three cells at one end, three at the other, and a large central cell with two nuclei |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) Meiosis of the megaspore mother cell

**(b)** 8

**(c)** (i) **Three** free-nuclear mitoses (1 → 2 → 4 → 8 nuclei). Six nuclei are walled off as cells (egg, two synergids, three antipodals), and the remaining **two polar nuclei** share one central cell, so there are 7 cells but 8 nuclei.

**OR** (ii) **Stage II**: of the four megaspores, three degenerate and only one develops, so the embryo sac comes from a single megaspore (monosporic). The micropylar end has the **egg cell and two synergids** (the egg apparatus).

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Stage I is the megaspore mother cell; it divides by meiosis into four megaspores (stage II) — option (d).

**(b)** Leaf cells have $2n = 16$, so $n = 16 \div 2 = 8$. The megaspore is haploid, and the sac nuclei come from it by mitosis, so each has 8.

**(c)** (i) Three doublings give 8 nuclei; the central cell holds two of them.

(ii) One of four megaspores survives; egg apparatus at the micropylar end.

Meiosis of the functional megaspore
Free-nuclear mitosis in the embryo sac
Meiosis of the megaspore mother cell

children.solution_md: Stage I is the megaspore mother cell; it divides by meiosis into four megaspores (stage II) — option (d).

children.stem_md: How many chromosomes would each nucleus in the stage IV sac contain?
children.solution_md: Leaf cells have $2n = 16$, so $n = 16 \div 2 = 8$. The megaspore is haploid, and the sac nuclei come from it by mitosis, so each has 8.

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): How many mitotic divisions separate the single functional megaspore from stage IV? Explain why the stage IV sac is described as having seven cells but eight nuclei.

answer.model_answer_md: **Three** free-nuclear mitoses (1 → 2 → 4 → 8 nuclei). Six nuclei are walled off as cells (egg, two synergids, three antipodals), and the remaining **two polar nuclei** share one central cell, so there are 7 cells but 8 nuclei.

children.solution_md: Three doublings give 8 nuclei; the central cell holds two of them.

marking_scheme.step: Two polar nuclei in one central cell: 7 cells, 8 nuclei

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Which stage shows that the embryo sac of this plant is monosporic? Explain, and name the three cells at the micropylar end of the stage IV sac.

answer.model_answer_md: **Stage II**: of the four megaspores, three degenerate and only one develops, so the embryo sac comes from a single megaspore (monosporic). The micropylar end has the **egg cell and two synergids** (the egg apparatus).

alternatives.solution_md: One of four megaspores survives; egg apparatus at the micropylar end.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A research station tested fruit set in a plant species with bisexual flowers. Each treatment was applied to 100 flowers on different plants, and the flowers that formed fruit were counted.

| Treatment | Flowers that set fruit |
|---|---|
| P: left open to visiting insects | 72 |
| Q: bagged, not emasculated | 5 |
| R: emasculated and bagged, no pollen added | 0 |
| S: emasculated, bagged, dusted with pollen from another plant | 81 |
| T: emasculated, bagged, dusted with pollen from another flower of the same plant | 4 |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (c) Q and T

**(b)** **Geitonogamy** (pollen from another flower of the same plant).

**(c)** (i) **Self-incompatibility.** The pistil recognises pollen from the same plant through chemical signals and blocks its germination or pollen-tube growth, so self-pollen (Q, T) rarely fertilises, while pollen from another plant (S) is accepted.

**OR** (ii) **For:** hand-pollination with pollen from another plant ensures enough compatible pollen reaches every stigma (81 against 72 fruits per 100 flowers), raising yield where insects are scarce. **Against:** it needs a lot of labour and time per flower, so on a large field the extra fruit may not pay for the cost; protecting insect pollinators is cheaper.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** In Q only the flower’s own pollen can reach the stigma, and in T the pollen comes from another flower of the same plant; both give very low fruit set — option (c).

**(b)** Another flower, same plant.

**(c)** (i) Low set with self-pollen but high set with other-plant pollen points to self-incompatibility.

(ii) Weigh the 9 percent gain against labour cost.

R and S

P and R

| Year | Seed source | Yield (quintals per hectare) | Field appearance |

answer.model_answer_md:

**(b)** 25 %
